lede: Put resistors in a line and their resistances add up. Put them side by side and the total drops below the smallest of them. This topic turns both facts into calculations, from a simple sum to a circuit that mixes the two.
can: Add resistors in series and halve an equal pair in parallel
Find the resistance of any two resistors in parallel with the Higher equation
Reduce a circuit with series and parallel sections to a single resistance

md: What matters to the supply is the total opposition of its resistors, and that depends on how they are joined as well as on their values.

caption: Same battery, same two resistors: in a line the total goes up, side by side it goes down.

md: The **total resistance** is the single resistor that could replace all of them and draw the same current from the supply.

**Why a smaller total means a bigger current.** The battery's voltage is fixed, and V = I R rearranges to $I = V \div R$. Halve the total resistance and the same battery drives twice the current; double it and the current halves.

stem: The figure joins the same two 33 Ω resistors to the same 6.6 V battery, first in series and then in parallel. Which arrangement has the smaller total resistance? [2]

steps.working: In series: $R = 33 + 33 = 66$ Ω, so the ammeter reads $6.6 \div 66 = 0.10$ A.
steps.decision: One route through both resistors: each adds its own opposition.

steps.working: In parallel the figure gives 16.5 Ω, so the ammeter reads $6.6 \div 16.5 = 0.40$ A, four times as much.
steps.decision: Two routes side by side: the same battery drives more current, so the parallel total is the smaller.

steps.working: One 33 Ω resistor alone would draw $6.6 \div 33 = 0.20$ A, the current of neither pair.
steps.decision: The near-miss: one resistor's value is the total of neither arrangement. The total is the single resistor that draws the same current as the whole.

prompt: A second resistor is connected in parallel with one already across a battery. What happens to the total resistance and to the current from the battery?
options: the total resistance falls and the current rises
the total resistance rises and the current falls
both stay the same, because the battery is the same
answer: the total resistance falls and the current rises
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, a resistor added side by side is a second route, so the same battery drives more current, and more current for the same voltage means a smaller total resistance. So the total falls and the current rises.

optionNotes.option: the total resistance rises and the current falls
optionNotes.why: More resistors feels like more opposition, but side by side the new one is an extra route, so more current flows and the total falls.

optionNotes.option: both stay the same, because the battery is the same
optionNotes.why: The battery sets the voltage, not the current: the new branch draws its own current from it, so the total current rises.

twin.prompt: A heater is joined in series with a lamp that is already lit by a supply. What happens to the total resistance and to the current from the supply?
options: the total resistance rises and the current falls
the total resistance falls and the current rises
both stay the same, because the supply is the same
twin.answer: the total resistance rises and the current falls
twin.explain: On one route the heater adds its own opposition, as the series pair did in step 1 of the See it: the total rises, so the same supply drives a smaller current.

optionNotes.option: the total resistance falls and the current rises
optionNotes.why: That is what a resistor added side by side does. In series the heater lies on the only route, so the total goes up.

optionNotes.option: both stay the same, because the supply is the same
optionNotes.why: The supply sets the voltage; a heater on the same route adds resistance, so less current flows.

text: 2. Why series adds and parallel shrinks

md: In series the same current has to pass through every resistor in turn, and the supply voltage is shared among them. Each resistor adds its own opposition to the one route, so the resistances add.
In parallel each extra branch is another route. It has the full voltage across it, so it carries extra current; the total current rises, and the total resistance falls below even the smallest branch.

title: The check that catches most slips
md: Two resistors in parallel always combine to less than the smaller of the two. If a parallel answer comes out bigger than either resistor, something has gone wrong.

stem: A 56 Ω resistor is connected across an 8.4 V battery, and a 168 Ω resistor is then connected in parallel with it. Explain why the total resistance falls. [3]

steps.working: On its own the 56 Ω resistor carries $8.4 \div 56 = 0.15$ A.
steps.decision: Current through a resistor is its voltage over its resistance (V = I R).

steps.working: The 168 Ω resistor also has the whole 8.4 V across it, so it carries $8.4 \div 168 = 0.05$ A, and the 56 Ω still carries 0.15 A.
steps.decision: Each branch is joined straight across the battery: a new branch adds a route and its own current, and takes nothing from the first.

steps.working: The battery now supplies $0.15 + 0.05 = 0.20$ A for the same 8.4 V, so the total is $8.4 \div 0.20 = 42$ Ω.
steps.decision: More current for the same voltage means less resistance: 42 Ω is below even the 56 Ω branch.

task: Connect one resistor across a battery with an ammeter in the main line and note the current. Predict the new reading, then add a second identical resistor in parallel and check. Finally put the two resistors in series instead and compare the three readings.

prompt: A 9 Ω resistor and a 72 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these could be their combined resistance?
options: 8 Ω
explain: As in step 3 of the See it, a second branch only adds current, so the total falls below even the smaller resistor, here 9 Ω. Only 8 Ω is below it: 81 Ω is the series total, and 40.5 Ω is half the sum, which fits only an equal pair.

optionNotes.why: Half the sum is the shortcut for two equal resistors. These are not equal, and side by side the total must be below 9 Ω.
That adds them, the series rule. A second branch is an extra route, so the total falls below the smaller resistor.

twin.prompt: A 7 Ω resistor and a 63 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Which of these could be their combined resistance?
twin.explain: Side by side, the total must be below the smaller resistor, 7 Ω, as the See it's pair fell below its smaller branch: only 6.3 Ω is. 70 Ω is the series total and 35 Ω half of it.

optionNotes.why: Half the sum fits only an equal pair; a parallel total is always below the smaller resistor, 7 Ω.
That is the series total; side by side the total falls below 7 Ω.

caption: In series the resistances simply add: the total is bigger than any one of them.

md: For resistors in series the total is the sum, $R = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$, for as many as there are. The total is always bigger than the biggest single resistor.

stem: In the figure, resistors of 33 Ω, 47 Ω and 68 Ω are connected in series between A and B. Calculate the total resistance between A and B. [1]

steps.decision: One route through all three: each adds its own opposition, so the equation adds them.
Add them in any order; the value with its unit earns the mark.

steps.working: Check: 148 Ω is bigger than 68 Ω, the largest of them.
steps.decision: A series total is always bigger than the biggest single resistor.

prompt: Resistors of 17 Ω, 19 Ω and 34 Ω are connected in series. What is their total resistance, in ohms?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, every resistor lies on the one route, so each adds its own opposition: 17 + 19 + 34 = 70 Ω, bigger than the largest of them, 34 Ω.

twin.prompt: Resistors of 26 Ω, 39 Ω and 51 Ω are connected in series. What is their total resistance, in ohms?
twin.explain: One route, so the resistances add: 26 + 39 + 51 = 116 Ω.

text: 4. Two equal resistors in parallel: halve one

caption: Two equal routes side by side: half the resistance of one of them.

md: Two **equal** resistors side by side give twice the route for the same voltage, so twice the current, so half the resistance: $R = R_1 \div 2$. The shortcut works only when the two resistors are equal.

title: The mark most Foundation candidates lost
md: Summer 2025 Foundation: a significant number found the series total of two 9 Ω resistors, but only the most able found their parallel total. Halve an equal pair; never add it.

stem: In the figure, two 86 Ω resistors are connected in parallel between A and B. Calculate their combined resistance. [1]

steps.decision: Two equal routes carry twice the current of one for the same voltage, so the pair has half the resistance of one.
Halve one of them; never add them.

steps.working: Check: 43 Ω is less than 86 Ω. Adding them, 172 Ω, would be the series rule.
steps.decision: The near-miss: a parallel total is always below the smaller resistor, so 172 Ω cannot be right.

prompt: A pair of equal 50 Ω resistors sits side by side between two terminals. What resistance do they give together, in ohms?
explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, two equal routes carry twice the current for the same voltage, so the pair has half the resistance of one: 50 ÷ 2 = 25 Ω, less than 50 Ω, as a parallel total must be.

twin.prompt: Two 82 Ω resistors are joined side by side, in parallel. What single resistance could replace them, in ohms?
twin.explain: An equal pair side by side has half the resistance of one: 82 ÷ 2 = 41 Ω.

caption: Unequal resistors in parallel: the total is less than the smaller one.

md: For two **unequal** resistors in parallel, Higher Tier uses $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2}$. The sum on the right gives $\dfrac{1}{R}$, not R, so the last step is always to turn the answer upside down.

**Why the reciprocals add.** Each branch carries its own current, $V \div R_1$ and $V \div R_2$, and the currents add. So it is one over each resistance that adds, not the resistances themselves (section 8 shows it in three lines), and the sum is 1/R.

stem: In the figure, a 35 Ω and a 140 Ω resistor are connected in parallel between A and B. Calculate their combined resistance. [3]

steps.decision: Write the Higher equation first: the equation line earns its own mark.
Substitute the two resistances.
Add over a common denominator, or add the decimals on a calculator. This is 1/R, not R yet.
Turn the sum upside down.
Product over sum gives the same value, and a parallel total is below the smaller resistor.

title: Resistors in series and parallel
why: Five minutes on total resistance in series and in parallel, and on using the total to find a current. It is made for another board, which may only say that a parallel total is less than either resistor; CCEA sets the calculation, as in sections 4 and 5. Its potential difference is CCEA's voltage.

prompt: A 5 Ω resistor and a 7.5 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance, in ohms?
explain: As in steps 2 to 4 of the See it, add the reciprocals, then turn the sum upside down: $\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{7.5} = \dfrac{5}{15}$, so R = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 Ω, less than 5 Ω.

twin.prompt: A 44 Ω resistor and a 66 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance, in ohms?
twin.explain: Add the reciprocals and invert: $\dfrac{1}{44} + \dfrac{1}{66} = \dfrac{5}{132}$, so R = 132 ÷ 5 = 26.4 Ω, below 44 Ω.

text: 6. See it done: one pair, both ways

md: The paper often gives one pair and asks for both totals. Work each with its own rule, then check both: the series total above the larger resistor, the parallel total below the smaller.

stem: A 34 Ω and a 51 Ω resistor are connected first in series and then in parallel. Calculate both totals. [4]

steps.decision: One route: the resistances add.
The Higher equation, with the values in.
Common denominator, then turn the sum upside down.

steps.working: Check: 85 Ω is above 51 Ω, and 20.4 Ω is below 34 Ω.
steps.decision: Both checks pass, so neither rule was swapped.

prompt: A 27 Ω resistor and a 108 Ω resistor are connected first in series and then in parallel. Which pair of totals is right?
options: 135 Ω in series, 21.6 Ω in parallel
135 Ω in series, 67.5 Ω in parallel
21.6 Ω in series, 135 Ω in parallel
answer: 135 Ω in series, 21.6 Ω in parallel
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of the See it, in series the two add: 27 + 108 = 135 Ω. In parallel add the reciprocals and invert: $\dfrac{1}{27} + \dfrac{1}{108} = \dfrac{5}{108}$, so R = 21.6 Ω, below 27 Ω.

optionNotes.option: 135 Ω in series, 67.5 Ω in parallel
optionNotes.why: Halving the sum is the equal-pair shortcut; 27 Ω and 108 Ω are not equal, and 67.5 Ω is above the smaller resistor.

optionNotes.option: 21.6 Ω in series, 135 Ω in parallel
optionNotes.why: The rules are swapped: a series total is above the larger resistor, and a parallel total below the smaller.

twin.prompt: A 39 Ω resistor and a 78 Ω resistor are connected first in series and then in parallel. Which pair of totals is right?
options: 117 Ω in series, 26 Ω in parallel
117 Ω in series, 58.5 Ω in parallel
26 Ω in series, 117 Ω in parallel
twin.answer: 117 Ω in series, 26 Ω in parallel
twin.explain: In series they add, 117 Ω. In parallel $\dfrac{1}{39} + \dfrac{1}{78} = \dfrac{3}{78}$, so R = 78 ÷ 3 = 26 Ω, below 39 Ω.

optionNotes.option: 117 Ω in series, 58.5 Ω in parallel
optionNotes.why: Half the sum fits only an equal pair; a parallel total must be below the smaller resistor, 39 Ω.

optionNotes.option: 26 Ω in series, 117 Ω in parallel
optionNotes.why: The rules are swapped: in series the total is above both resistors, in parallel below both.

caption: Box the parallel pair, replace it by one value, then add along the line.

md: When a circuit has a series part and a parallel part, deal with the parallel section first. Replace the pair by the single resistance it is equivalent to, then add the series resistors along the line. Never add a parallel pair straight into the total.

**Why the pair comes first.** The series rule adds resistors that carry the same current. Neither branch of the pair carries the whole current; only the two together do, so the pair must become one value before anything is added to it.

stem: In the figure, a 29 Ω resistor is in series with a 57 Ω and a 114 Ω resistor that are in parallel with each other. Calculate the total resistance between A and B. [3]

steps.decision: Box the parallel section and deal with it first.
Turn the sum upside down: the pair acts as one 38 Ω resistor.
Now the circuit is one line: add along it.

steps.working: Check: adding all three, 200 Ω, would treat the pair as if it were in series.
steps.decision: The near-miss: a parallel pair never goes straight into the sum.

prompt: A 9 Ω resistor is connected in series with two 10 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. What is the total resistance, in ohms?
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of the See it, reduce the parallel pair first: two equal 10 Ω resistors give 10 ÷ 2 = 5 Ω. Then add along the line: 9 + 5 = 14 Ω. Adding all three, 29 Ω, would treat the pair as series.

twin.prompt: A 41 Ω resistor is connected in series with two 34 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. What is the total resistance, in ohms?
twin.explain: The equal pair first: 34 ÷ 2 = 17 Ω. Then add along the line: 41 + 17 = 58 Ω.

text: 8. Where the parallel equation comes from

caption: The parallel rules, written in symbols: one voltage V, and a current that splits.

md: Two rules from the series and parallel topic give the parallel equation in three lines: the branch currents add up, and every branch has the supply voltage across it.
Series comes out the same way: the voltages add, $IR = IR_1 + IR_2$, and dividing by the one current I gives $R = R_1 + R_2$.

stem: Use the rules for a parallel circuit to show that $\dfrac{1}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2}$ for two resistors in parallel. [3]

steps.decision: The branch currents add up to the current from the supply.
Every branch has the same voltage V, and each current is V over its resistance.
V is in every term, so it divides out.

steps.working: Check: 35 Ω and 140 Ω on 7.0 V carry 0.20 A and 0.05 A, 0.25 A in all, so $R = 7.0 \div 0.25 = 28$ Ω.
steps.decision: The same value as the equation gave in section 5.

prompt: In the derivation of the parallel equation, why can V be divided out of every term?
options: every branch has the same voltage as the supply across it
the current is the same in every branch
V is always equal to 1 volt
answer: every branch has the same voltage as the supply across it
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, one V stands for the voltage of the whole pair and of each branch, because in parallel every branch is joined straight across the supply. A factor in every term divides out. The branch currents differ, which is why they add.

optionNotes.option: the current is the same in every branch
optionNotes.why: That is the series rule. In parallel the branch currents differ, which is why step 1 adds them; the voltage is what every branch shares.

optionNotes.option: V is always equal to 1 volt
optionNotes.why: V can be any voltage. It divides out because the same V stands in every term, not because it is 1.

twin.prompt: The series equation comes from IR = IR₁ + IR₂. Why can I be divided out of every term?
options: the same current passes through every resistor in series
every resistor in series has the supply voltage across it
the current is always 1 ampere
twin.answer: the same current passes through every resistor in series
twin.explain: In series there is one route, so one current I passes through every resistor. A factor in every term divides out, leaving R = R₁ + R₂.

optionNotes.option: every resistor in series has the supply voltage across it
optionNotes.why: In series the supply voltage is shared, not repeated; what every resistor shares is the one current.

optionNotes.option: the current is always 1 ampere
optionNotes.why: I can be any current; it divides out because it stands in every term.

md: **Build a total from given resistors.** Summer 2019 and Summer 2023 Higher gave three resistors and the totals to reach. Try the moves in turn: add in series, halve an equal pair, combine an unequal pair, one in series with a pair.

**Switches** (Summer 2021 Higher, Summer 2022 Foundation). A closed switch across a resistor carries the current round it, so that resistor adds nothing; an open switch in a branch takes that branch out.
**Use your answer to (i).** Summer 2021 and 2023: combine the pair first, reuse it, then share the current between the branches.

stem: In the figure, switches K and L are both open. Find the resistance between X and Y. [2]

steps.working: L open: its branch carries no current, so of the pair only the other 8 Ω resistor is left.
steps.decision: An open switch in a branch takes that branch out of the circuit.

steps.working: K open: the current must pass through the 7 Ω resistor, so it adds: $7 + 8 = 15$ Ω.
steps.decision: An open switch carries no current, so the resistor beside it stays in the line.

steps.working: Closed, K would carry the current round the 7 Ω resistor, and that resistor would add nothing.
steps.decision: A closed switch is a path of almost no resistance beside the resistor.

prompt: In the circuit shown, switches K and L are both closed. What is the resistance between X and Y, in ohms?
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of the See it, take each switch in turn. K closed carries the current round the 7 Ω resistor, so it adds nothing. L closed brings its 8 Ω branch in beside the other 8 Ω: an equal pair, 8 ÷ 2 = 4 Ω.

twin.prompt: In the same circuit, K is open and L is closed. What is the resistance between X and Y, in ohms?
twin.explain: K open keeps the 7 Ω in the line; L closed makes the two 8 Ω resistors an equal pair of 4 Ω: 7 + 4 = 11 Ω.

caption: Working backwards: one resistor in series, and a pair that makes up the rest.

md: Summer 2023 Higher gave the resistors and the total and asked for the arrangement. Work backwards: a total above every resistor needs one in series; below the smallest, a parallel pair. In between, try a pair alone, then one resistor plus a pair.

title: Where the specification stops
md: CCEA asks for any two resistors in parallel; three or more all in parallel go beyond the specification.

stem: A pupil has a 44 Ω resistor and two 132 Ω resistors. Find an arrangement with a total resistance of 165 Ω. [2]

steps.working: 165 Ω is bigger than 132 Ω, so one 132 Ω goes in series, leaving $165 - 132 = 33$ Ω to find.
steps.decision: A total above every resistor needs one in series.

steps.working: 44 Ω and 132 Ω in parallel: $44 \times 132 \div 176 = 33$ Ω.
steps.decision: The two left over, side by side, make up the rest.

steps.working: So: one 132 Ω in series with the 44 Ω and the other 132 Ω in parallel, as in the figure.
steps.decision: Check that the arrangement uses each resistor once.

prompt: A pupil has a 9 Ω resistor and two 38 Ω resistors. Which arrangement gives a total of 28 Ω?
options: the 9 Ω resistor in series with the two 38 Ω resistors in parallel
one 38 Ω resistor in series with the 9 Ω and the other 38 Ω in parallel
all three resistors in series
answer: the 9 Ω resistor in series with the two 38 Ω resistors in parallel
explain: As in steps 1 and 2 of the See it, work backwards from 28 Ω. It is below 38 Ω, so no 38 Ω can stand alone in series. Two 38 Ω in parallel give 19 Ω, and 9 + 19 = 28 Ω.

optionNotes.option: one 38 Ω resistor in series with the 9 Ω and the other 38 Ω in parallel
optionNotes.why: That arrangement starts from 38 Ω, already above the 28 Ω target, so it gives about 45 Ω.

optionNotes.option: all three resistors in series
optionNotes.why: Three in series add to 85 Ω, far above 28 Ω; a target below 38 Ω needs a parallel pair.

twin.prompt: A pupil has an 8 Ω resistor and two 56 Ω resistors. Which arrangement gives a total of 63 Ω?
options: one 56 Ω resistor in series with the 8 Ω and the other 56 Ω in parallel
the 8 Ω resistor in series with the two 56 Ω resistors in parallel
all three resistors in series
twin.answer: one 56 Ω resistor in series with the 8 Ω and the other 56 Ω in parallel
twin.explain: 63 Ω is above 56 Ω, so one 56 Ω goes in series, leaving 7 Ω; 8 Ω and 56 Ω in parallel give 448 ÷ 64 = 7 Ω.

optionNotes.option: the 8 Ω resistor in series with the two 56 Ω resistors in parallel
optionNotes.why: That gives 8 + 28 = 36 Ω, below the target; 63 Ω is above 56 Ω, so one 56 Ω must stand in series.

optionNotes.option: all three resistors in series
optionNotes.why: That gives 120 Ω, far above 63 Ω.

md:
Add every resistance in series.
Halve an equal pair in parallel.
Combine any two in parallel (Higher): add the reciprocals, then turn the sum upside down.
Reduce a parallel section first, then add along the line.
Check every parallel total: it is less than the smaller resistor.

Resistance totals come as one- to three-mark parts inside a circuit question that goes on to a current with V = I R. For a Higher parallel pair, write the equation first; the last mark is the value after turning it upside down. Stuck? Ask whether the resistors share one route or several, and check a parallel answer against the smaller resistor.
